summary: In Canada, a refundable SR&ED investment tax credit is paid in cash, while a non-refundable credit reduces federal Part I tax payable. Qualifying CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations earn a 35% credit, fully refundable on up to $6 million of current expenditures; foreign-controlled and other public corporations receive 15% non-refundable credits.

Qualifying CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations earn a 35% credit, fully refundable on up to $6 million of current expenditures; foreign-controlled and other public corporations receive 15% non-refundable credits.
Executive Summary and the 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation

Canada operates one of the most mature, statutory-entitlement research and development tax incentive frameworks in the industrialised world through the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually, the federal SR&ED architecture provides a dual-pillar fiscal benefit: first, an immediate 100% income tax deduction (or indefinite carryforward) for allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures pooled under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act; and second, an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated on qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), which may be refunded in cash under section 127.1 or applied to reduce federal Part I tax payable. When stacked with provincial and territorial R&D tax credits across Canada's federated tax system, combined federal-provincial support routinely offsets between 40% and 65% of eligible domestic R&D labour and overhead outlays.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential statutory expansion in more than a decade. Following policy consultations initiated in Budget 2024, the federal government unveiled sweeping structural reforms in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024, published draft legislative proposals on August 15, 2025, confirmed the framework in Budget 2025 (Canada Strong), and enacted the measures into law through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Simultaneously, at the provincial level, the Government of Québec enacted a foundational overhaul in its March 25, 2025 budget, abolishing its legacy R&D salary and partnership credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 and replacing them with the consolidated, fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC).

body.text: The policy architecture enacted through Bill C-15 addresses three long-standing structural bottlenecks in Canadian innovation finance. First, by doubling the annual expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million and shifting the taxable capital phase-out band upward from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, Parliament reversed over a decade of inflationary erosion that had prematurely pushed scaling mid-sized enterprises out of the refundable regime. Second, by allowing CCPCs to elect annually into the three-year average gross revenue phase-out methodology ($15 million to $75 million) designed for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the legislation eliminates the punitive "balance-sheet penalty" that previously stripped venture-backed biotechnology, semiconductor, clean technology, and hardware companies of their refundable 35% credits simply because they raised substantial equity or debt capital prior to commercialization. Third, the restoration of depreciable capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 directly targets capital-intensive R&D—including artificial intelligence compute clusters (such as graphics processing units), pilot-scale manufacturing tooling, and specialized laboratory instrumentation—aligning the SR&ED regime with modern hardware-software convergence.
Federal Statutory and Regulatory Framework
The Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. For an activity to qualify, it must comprise a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and fall within one of four enumerated operational categories while avoiding seven statutory exclusions.

Within the four affirmative categories of subsection 248(1), paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in academic, institutional, or specialized corporate laboratories—for example, characterizing the molecular properties of a newly discovered virus or pathogen—and represents the smallest share of corporate claims. Paragraph 248(1)(b) covers applied research, which is work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as investigating immunological mechanisms to formulate a targeted vaccine against a newly characterized virus. Paragraph 248(1)(c) governs experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of Canadian corporate SR&ED claims, encompassing process scale-up, material formulation, hardware prototyping, and complex algorithmic or systems engineering. Finally, paragraph 248(1)(d) incorporates eligible support work, which comprises work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs—in amount, size, extent, and duration—and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial and routine technical activities from constituting SR&ED, even if they occur within an innovative enterprise or adjacent to an R&D project. Specifically, the statute excludes market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph (f); research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas under paragraph (h); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i); style changes under paragraph (j); and routine data collection under paragraph (k), unless the data collection is performed specifically and directly to support eligible SR&ED work under paragraph (d). In addition to these statutory exclusions, CRA administrative policy emphasizes that activities aimed at acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists in the public domain or within the industry—including employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring consultants or specialists to apply existing expertise, or purchasing proprietary third-party technology—do not seek a scientific or technological advancement and are therefore ineligible.
The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act establishes a dedicated tax accounting mechanism—the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures—for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer. Unlike ordinary business expenses governed by section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) (which must be deducted in the year incurred and where capital outlays are barred by paragraph 18(1)(b)), subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer to aggregate all allowable current SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) and allowable SR&ED capital expenditures (for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) under paragraph 37(1)(b) into a cumulative pool.

The mechanics of the subsection 37(1) pool operate through a continuous additions-and-deductions formula at the end of each taxation year. On the additions side of the ledger, the pool is increased by allowable current expenditures on SR&ED directly undertaken in Canada by the taxpayer under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), payments for SR&ED performed on behalf of the taxpayer under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), and eligible third-party payments to corporations or approved entities under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii). The pool is further increased by allowable capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024 to acquire depreciable property intended for all-or-substantially-all (ASA) SR&ED use or consumption in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(b), as well as repayments made by the taxpayer in the year of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c). On the subtractions side of the ledger, paragraph 37(1)(d) reduces the pool by all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Paragraph 37(1)(e) then deducts federal SR&ED investment tax credits claimed (whether deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash) in the immediately preceding taxation year, along with the amount deducted by the taxpayer from the pool in computing net income for tax purposes in the preceding taxation year.

Any positive balance in the subsection 37(1) pool at the end of the taxation year may be deducted in full or in part in computing the taxpayer's income for the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years (subject to acquisition-of-control streaming restrictions under subsection 37(6.1)). If subtractions (such as prior-year federal ITCs or current-year assistance) exceed additions and cause the pool balance to become negative at year-end, the negative balance must be included in the taxpayer's income under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Act.
The Section 127 Investment Tax Credit and Section 127.1 Refundability Architecture

While section 37 governs the deductibility of R&D costs from taxable income, section 127 governs the calculation of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC), and section 127.1 governs its cash refundability. Under subsection 127(9), the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" is calculated annually at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over as an expenditure pool to subsequent years; rather, it converts into an ITC at the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures are incurred.

body.text: The mathematical determination of the annual expenditure limit and its phase-out under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 is anchored by a base expenditure limit of $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024), which is pro-rated for taxation years shorter than 365 days (or 366 days in a leap year) and shared among all associated corporations via Schedule T2SCH49. Under the default taxable capital phase-out formula applicable to CCPCs, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of Part I.3 of the Act) of the corporation and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000. Where Taxable Capital<sub>t-1</sub> represents the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated group. For every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000, the expenditure limit decreases by $1.

As an alternative to the taxable capital test, under the Bill C-15 amendments to subsections 127(9) and 127(10.2), an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—defined as a corporation resident in Canada, listed on a designated Canadian stock exchange, and not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by non-resident persons—is subject to a mandatory three-year average gross revenue phase-out test, while a CCPC may elect on an annual basis to calculate its expenditure limit reduction using this same revenue methodology whenever it yields a higher limit than prior-year taxable capital. Under this gross revenue test, the phase-out is computed using the average annual gross revenue reflected in the financial statements (prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles) of the corporation and all associated group members over the three preceding fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year window. Reasonable adjustments are permitted to eliminate intra-group sales of goods or services so that the consolidated revenue reflects that of a single economic entity. The gross revenue phase-out applies across the identical $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 band:
Expenditure Limit<sub>Revenue</sub> = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − max(0, min($60,000,000, Avg. Annual Revenue − $15,000,000))) ÷ $60,000,000

Any SR&ED ITC that is refunded in cash under subsection 127.1(1) is deemed by subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable for the year, thereby reducing the remaining ITC pool available for carryback or carryforward. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5). No SR&ED ITC may be earned on expenditures incurred in the course of earning income that is exempt from Part I tax under section 149.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
Current Expenditures: Direct Labour, Specified Employees, and Support Staff

Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9), eligible salary or wages encompass remuneration paid to employees of the claimant who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Directly engaged duties include hands-on scientific experimentation, engineering analysis, direct first-line technical supervision of experimental work, and technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the taxation year (such as assigning technological personnel, establishing experimental priorities, formulating technological strategies, and specifying material quality tolerances). Furthermore, tasks performed by non-specialized or shop-floor employees—such as operating a machine required for an experimental trial or feeding raw materials into an experimental line—qualify as direct SR&ED labour provided those employees are directly supervised by staff possessing scientific or technological qualifications.

A critical statutory distinction governs specified employees versus arm's-length (non-specified) employees. Under subsection 248(1), a "specified employee" is an employee who is a specified shareholder of the corporation (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer.

body.text: Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

The CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy divides eligible material outlays into two distinct categories: materials consumed and materials transformed. Materials consumed during SR&ED are materials that are destroyed, used up, absorbed, evaporated, or broken down into small pieces such that they are rendered virtually valueless as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED. General items such as cleaning supplies, broken or used laboratory glassware, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants (such as engine oil), and general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas) do not qualify as materials consumed. However, if a utility such as water is physically consumed as a reactant or constituent in an SR&ED chemical process rather than used as a general facility utility, the claimant may claim the cost as materials consumed provided the portion is clearly identified, documented, and allocated using a reasonable, supportable, and verifiable methodology.

By contrast, materials transformed are materials that are integrated into another product, prototype, experimental production run, pilot plant, or commercial asset during the course of SR&ED that retains some economic value at the conclusion of the experiment. While 100% of the cost of materials transformed is initially eligible for the section 37 deduction and section 127 ITC in the year the material is transformed, any subsequent sale of the resulting property or conversion of the property to commercial use triggers the statutory Recapture of ITC rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(36).
Overhead and Other Expenditures: The Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Election

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, every claimant must elect annually between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method for computing SR&ED overhead expenditures. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method is irrevocable for that taxation year.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically track, itemize, or deduct SR&ED overhead costs within the section 37 pool (instead deducting general overhead expenses as ordinary business expenses under section 9). For purposes of calculating the section 127 Investment Tax Credit, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 under Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations and subsection 127(9) of the Act. The PPA is equal to 55% of the claimant's eligible "salary base" (comprising the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, unpaid amounts, and subject to the 2.5 × YMPE cap for specified employees and the overall PPA cap). Because the PPA is a statutory substitute covering general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), clerical and administrative support staff salaries, office supplies, utilities, and facility overhead, the claimant cannot separately claim these items on Form T661 when electing the proxy method. The PPA is frequently greater than the actual incremental overhead incurred by software, engineering, and life sciences firms, making the proxy method the dominant election across Canadian industry.

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated. Instead, pursuant to paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate all overhead and other expenditures (reported on Line 360 of Form T661) that are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. An expenditure is "directly attributable" only where it is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED—meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred had the SR&ED work not taken place. The traditional method is typically advantageous only for manufacturing or heavy-industrial claimants where SR&ED is conducted predominantly by third-party contractors or where massive incremental facility utilities, shop-floor support labour, or partial-use equipment leases (<50% SR&ED use) dwarf direct internal R&D payroll.
Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

The tax treatment of external R&D expenditures depends strictly on whether the work is performed under an SR&ED contract or as a third-party payment, and whether the parties deal at arm's length under section 251 of the Income Tax Act. When a claimant enters into an arm's-length SR&ED contract (governed by subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9)) with an arm's-length "taxable supplier" (a Canadian resident individual, partnership, or corporation, or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the contract cost is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, and 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies for the federal ITC under subsection 127(9). The statutory 20% haircut removes the subcontractor's notional profit margin from the ITC base. Foreign subcontractors performing work outside Canada are completely ineligible for SR&ED incentives.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted under a non-arm's-length (NAL) contract, subsection 127(11.6) and the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy dictate that payments made to a non-arm's-length contractor can be deducted in the payer's section 37 pool, but 0% of the payment qualifies directly for an ITC in the hands of the payer. Instead, the NAL performer incurs the underlying qualified expenditures and may either claim the ITC itself or execute a joint election with the NAL payer under subsection 127(13) (Form T1146) to transfer all or part of the qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount, reported on Lines 535 and 540 of Form T661) to the payer. Furthermore, under the subsection 37(14) look-through rule, if a contract includes both SR&ED and non-SR&ED deliverables or capital property, expenditures must be disaggregated according to the underlying nature of the property or service.

Distinct from SR&ED subcontracts—where the contractor performs work on behalf of the claimant under the claimant's technical direction and intellectual property ownership—a third-party payment under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) is a payment made to an approved entity (such as an approved university, college, research institute, approved association, granting council, or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada) for SR&ED carried on in Canada where the work relates to a business of the claimant and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the research. Exactly like arm's-length contracts, 100% of a third-party payment is deductible under section 37 and 80% is included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9). The claimant must complete and file Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.
Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Pursuant to Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, expenditures for depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024, determined by when the property becomes available for use and where ownership or a leasehold interest is obtained) and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 are once again eligible for SR&ED tax incentives. Capital and lease expenditures made before December 16, 2024 remain permanently ineligible.

body.text: To substantiate capital and lease claims, the CRA mandates rigorous contemporaneous evidence of intent at the time of acquisition alongside operational usage logs. On the revised Form T661, claimants must report the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024 for each project on Lines 262 and 263 of Part 2, and detail the 20 most expensive depreciable properties and shared-use equipment items across the entire claim in Boxes 780, 782, and 788 of Part 6. Claimants must also account for the proposed federal Productivity Mega Deduction announced in September 2026—which permits immediate 100% expensing for most new depreciable capital property (including software and computer hardware) acquired on or after September 15, 2026—by ensuring that any capital asset claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 is excluded from Schedule 8 (Capital Cost Allowance) so as not to violate the statutory prohibition against double deductions.
Government Assistance, Contract Payments, Unpaid Amounts, and Recapture of ITCs

Three statutory anti-windfall mechanisms protect the integrity of the SR&ED tax base: the reduction for assistance and contract payments, the 180-day unpaid amounts rule, and the 20-year ITC recapture regime. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19), any government assistance (including direct federal or provincial grants, forgivable loans, subsidies, and provincial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), or "contract payment" that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year reduces both the section 37 deductible expenditure pool and section 127 qualified expenditures. Under subsection 127(9), a contract payment is an amount paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's-length Canadian "taxable supplier" (or by a Canadian federal, provincial, or municipal government or public authority, or a Part I tax-exempt entity under section 149) for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of that payer. If assistance and contract payments exceed a project's SR&ED expenditures, subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's-length group members on that project to nil (allocable via Form T1145). Crucially, if a Canadian R&D company performs contract R&D for a foreign (non-resident) client that does not carry on business through a permanent establishment in Canada, the foreign client is not a "taxable supplier" under subsection 127(9); consequently, the revenue received from the foreign client is not a "contract payment" and does not reduce the Canadian performer's SR&ED qualified expenditures.

Furthermore, a powerful statutory leverage effect arises from the interaction of direct government grants—such as wage subsidies from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—with the 55% Proxy Method. When a claimant receives an NRC IRAP grant and elects the Proxy Method, the grant reduces total qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 513 of Part 4 of Form T661, not the eligible direct SR&ED salary base in Part 5 used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). For example, if a qualifying CCPC incurs $100,000 in direct SR&ED salaries and receives a $60,000 NRC IRAP grant, the PPA is still computed on the full $100,000 salary base (PPA = $55,000), creating $155,000 in gross expenditures; deducting the $60,000 grant leaves $95,000 in net qualified SR&ED expenditures—more than double the company's $40,000 net out-of-pocket cash outlay. When any government or non-government assistance is subsequently repaid, paragraph 37(1)(c), paragraphs 127(9)(e.1) and (e.2), and subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8) restore the deduction pool and regenerate the ITC at the historical rate that applied in the year the assistance originally reduced the claim.

With respect to unpaid outlays and asset dispositions, subsection 127(26) stipulates that any non-salary SR&ED expenditure remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that year and is instead deemed incurred at the time it is paid in a subsequent year (whereas unpaid salary or wages after 180 days are permanently denied SR&ED treatment under subsection 78(4)). Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the CRA's Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant disposes of, or converts to commercial use, any property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned—including materials transformed into a commercial product or custom asset, ASA capital equipment, shared-use equipment (SUE), or property acquired under an SR&ED contract or non-arm's-length section 127(13) transfer—within 20 years of acquisition, the claimant must include in its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion a recapture amount equal to the lesser of: (a) the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the property, and (b) the historical ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion to commercial use). Note that under the CRA's Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy, the sale or licensing of intellectual property (IP) generated during an SR&ED project does not trigger ITC recapture, because IP is an intangible output rather than the physical property or material on which the expenditure was incurred.
Judicial Precedents and the CRA Administrative Eligibility Framework
The Canonical "Five Questions" of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen

The foundational judicial authority governing the interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is the seminal 1998 Tax Court of Canada decision by Justice (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC). Reviewing Information Circular IC 86-4R3, Justice Bowman articulated five cumulative questions that Canadian courts apply to determine whether a project constitutes eligible SR&ED—a test subsequently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998), C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, National R&D Inc. v. Canada, and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada.

First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; Justice Bowman emphasized that if the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using established engineering methodologies, reference manuals, or standard professional practice known to a competent professional in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, if such uncertainty existed, the court asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, requiring a testable scientific or technological proposition directed at overcoming the specific limitation identified. Third, the court examines whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through structured observation, experimental design, iterative testing, analysis of variables, and logical deduction rather than ad hoc trial-and-error or intuitive debugging. Fourth, the court evaluates whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—an advancement in general understanding in the field—noting that even when a project fails to meet its commercial or functional target, the rigorous elimination of a plausible technological hypothesis still constitutes a valid technological advancement by proving what does not work and why. Fifth, the court asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed, requiring contemporaneous evidence generated during the course of the investigation.
Evolution of CRA Guidelines ("Why and How") vs. Contemporary Tax Court Jurisprudence

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and issued the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives. The updated CRA guidelines reorganize the five questions of Northwest Hydraulic into two overarching requirements designed to provide a simplified common vocabulary during administrative reviews. Under the first requirement—the "Why" requirement (scientific or technological advancement)—the CRA evaluates why the work was conducted, requiring that it be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement (seeking to generate new knowledge that resolves a scientific or technological uncertainty rather than merely achieving a commercial or functional product objective). Under the second requirement—the "How" requirement (systematic investigation or search)—the CRA evaluates how the work was conducted, requiring that it be carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis following four sequential steps: defining a scientific or technological problem or uncertainty; advancing a hypothesis towards resolving that problem; planning and testing the hypothesis by experiment or analysis; and developing logical conclusions based on the results, supported by contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

Despite the CRA's administrative shift to the "Why and How" terminology, recent jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal confirms that the common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding legal standard in Canadian courts.

headers: Judicial Holding & Precedential Impact for Audits

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC)
Foundational criteria for defining SR&ED under s. 248(1) in hydraulic physical modelling projects.
Established the canonical Five Questions test; held that tax incentives for SR&ED must be given a fair, large, and liberal interpretation that best ensures the attainment of Parliament's object.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 & RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 FCA)
Appellate endorsement of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria and evidentiary standards.
Formally adopted Justice Bowman's Five Questions as the binding appellate standard across Canada.
Characterization of contract work and "contract payments" under s. 127(9).
Clarified the analysis of contractual substance when determining whether payments received by a claimant constitute "contract payments" that reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures.
Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 & National R&D / PTS Project, 2020 TCC 47
Whether Question 5 of Northwest Hydraulic mandates strict documentary records versus credible oral testimony.

Held (at para. 118 of Formadrain and paras. 65–67 of 2020 TCC 47) that the Income Tax Act does not explicitly require all evidence to be documentary; while lack of documentation is risky, credible testimonial evidence supported by contemporaneous notes can satisfy Question 5.
Zeuter Development Corp. v. The Queen (2021 TCC) & LES Services Technologiques v. Quebec (2020)
Software engineering eligibility and lack of contemporaneous experimental records.
Denied software SR&ED claims where claimants failed to produce contemporaneous documentation proving systematic hypothesis testing beyond standard software development.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025/2026 TCC, Justice Bodie)
Food science SR&ED claim (2020 tax year) for developing a shelf-stable vinegar-based beverage ("Chrisoda") using known preservatives (potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and "Chiber").

Allowed the taxpayer's appeal; held that (1) the Five Questions remain the valid judicial test notwithstanding the CRA's "Why and How" policy; (2) technological uncertainty can exist even when using publicly known ingredients/solutions if never applied in that specific context; and (3) contemporaneous records need only track hypotheses, tests, and results for the claimant, not enable an uninitiated outsider to replicate the experiment.

body.text: The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King is particularly instructive for audit defence. During administrative reviews, CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) frequently disallow claims on the grounds that individual components, chemical agents, or software libraries utilized by the claimant were publicly known to competent professionals, or that the claimant's lab notebooks were not formatted like peer-reviewed academic papers enabling third-party replication. Justice Bodie rejected both arguments, holding on a balance of probabilities that combining known components into a novel, unpredictable system interface creates genuine technological uncertainty when routine engineering cannot predict the interaction, and that internal experimental logs tracking iterative tests and microbial outcomes fully discharge the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Canada's provinces and territories supplement the federal SR&ED program with independent corporate income tax credits. Except in Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA through the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. Importantly, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal Income Tax Act, reducing the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified expenditures in the year the provincial credit is earned (unless the taxpayer validly waives or renounces the provincial credit).

Following the enactment of the federal Bill C-15 enhancements on March 26, 2026, provincial alignment has been bifurcated between "followers" and "holdouts". While provincial regimes whose statutory definitions automatically incorporate federal "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) absorb the restoration of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, provinces with standalone statutory expenditure caps—such as Ontario ($3 million OITC limit) and Alberta ($4 million IEG limit)—maintain their distinct provincial limits and phase-out formulas, whereas British Columbia's Budget 2026 amendments raised its refundable expenditure limit to $6 million and its taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15 million–$75 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

body.text: Québec's 2025/2026 Structural Overhaul: The CRIC Regime

Québec's Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC), enacted following the March 25, 2025 Québec budget for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, represents a paradigm shift in provincial innovation policy. Previously, Québec fragmented its R&D support across four separate refundable credits—the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V)—alongside the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, the industrial design tax credit, and the individual Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts. All of these legacy measures have been abolished for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 and consolidated into the single CRIC framework.

The CRIC introduces four structural innovations that distinguish Québec from every other Canadian jurisdiction. First, it establishes universal corporate access to the 30% enhanced rate regardless of asset size: whereas the former RD-1029.7 regime restricted the 30% enhanced rate to SMEs with consolidated worldwide assets below $50 million (phasing down to 14% at $75 million), under the CRIC every eligible corporation—regardless of total assets or paid-up capital—earns a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of net eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and a 20% fully refundable credit on all excess eligible expenditures (up from 14%). If a corporation claims the CRIC as a member of a partnership, its percentage interest is applied to the partnership's eligible expenditures, the 30% enhanced rate does not apply to the partnership share (which earns the 20% base rate), and individuals and trusts are excluded from claiming the CRIC.

Second, the CRIC expands the substantive scope of subsidized innovation to include pre-commercialization activities. Unlike the federal SR&ED program—which terminates once technological uncertainty is resolved and excludes commercial design, regulatory trials, and market-readiness validation under paragraph 248(1)(i)—the CRIC explicitly subsidizes pre-commercialization expenditures incurred in Québec, including product design, technological validations, prototyping, and regulatory or homologation testing, provided those activities are carried out as a direct continuation of R&D previously performed in Québec by or on behalf of the claimant. Third, the CRIC restores the eligibility of capital property, covering new depreciable capital property (excluding land, buildings, or rights in a building) acquired and made available for use in Québec almost exclusively (90% or more) in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

Fourth, the CRIC replaces the old sliding-scale bi-level threshold with a modified exclusion threshold under which only eligible expenditures exceeding the annual threshold generate the tax credit. The exclusion threshold is equal to the greater of: (a) $50,000 (pro-rated for short taxation years), or (b) the sum of the employee threshold for R&D employees and the employee threshold for pre-commercialization employees, calculated by multiplying the Québec basic personal amount for the calendar year by the proportion of working time each employee devotes to eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. Corporations claim the CRIC by filing Form RD-222-V (for the R&D deduction), Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (reporting the R&D portion under Code 112 and the pre-commercialization portion under Code 113 on the CO-17 corporate return), and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (detailing pre-commercialization activities). Crucially, only the R&D portion (Code 112, Line 180 of Form RD-1029.8.CR) reduces the Québec RD-222 pool (Line 71) and the federal Form T661 pools (Lines 429 and 513) as government assistance, because the pre-commercialization portion (Code 113) is not received in respect of federal SR&ED.
Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta: Navigating Provincial Expenditure Thresholds

Because Ontario and Alberta have retained their existing provincial expenditure limits and phase-out thresholds following the enactment of federal Bill C-15, while British Columbia has aligned its credit with the federal changes, multi-jurisdictional tax modelling requires careful attention to provincial-federal divergences. In Ontario, the 8% refundable OITC (Schedule 566) remains capped at $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario expenditures and phases out not only between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified paid-up capital, but also when prior-year federal taxable income of the associated group is between $500,000 and $800,000. Consequently, a profitable CCPC earning $850,000 in taxable income (or an ECPC) qualifies for the 35% refundable federal ITC on up to $6,000,000 of expenditures under Bill C-15, but receives $0 in Ontario OITC and is limited to the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508). Furthermore, if a corporation has no current Ontario corporate income tax payable (for instance, due to non-capital loss carryforwards) and claims the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC to carry forward, that unutilized ORDTC still constitutes "government assistance" in the current year under subsection 127(9) of the federal Act—reducing the federal 35% refundable ITC base immediately by 3.5% (a cash loss of 35% × 3.5% = 1.225% of total expenditures) in exchange for an illiquid paper carryforward. To prevent this value destruction, Ontario's Taxation Act, 2007 allows a corporation to deliver a formal written waiver of the ORDTC (or OITC) with its T2 return within 6 months of its taxation year-end (or on an amended return).

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit—administered by the CRA via Form T666 under Part 6 (sections 97 to 102.6) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act—provides a 10% refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of BC qualified expenditures ($600,000 maximum refund) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 and a 10% non-refundable credit on excess expenditures (with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward). In 2026, British Columbia permanently removed the former September 1, 2027 statutory expiry date, raised the taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, and expanded refundable credit eligibility to eligible Canadian public corporations. Similar to Ontario, subsection 100(1) of the BC Act allows a corporation to renounce all or part of its unused non-refundable BC SR&ED credit so that it does not erode the federal qualified expenditure pool.

In Alberta, under Division 7 of Part 6 (sections 26.95 to 26.99) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1R1, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29) awards an 8% refundable credit on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's "base amount" (the average of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years) and an enhanced 20% refundable credit (8% base plus 12% incremental bonus) on eligible expenditures exceeding the two-year base amount, up to a maximum expenditure limit of $4,000,000. For a first-time Alberta R&D performer (or a corporation with $0 in Alberta R&D spending during the prior two years), the two-year historical base amount is $0, meaning the entire first year of eligible Alberta R&D spending (up to $4,000,000) earns the full 20% refundable rate ($800,000 cash grant). In year two, the base becomes 50% of year one's spending, creating a dynamic two-year rolling oscillation that requires multi-year expenditure timing optimization.
Filing Procedures, Statutory Deadlines, Penalties, and CRA Audit Architecture
Prescribed Forms and the Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer cannot deduct an expenditure in the section 37 pool or include it in qualified expenditures for an ITC unless the taxpayer files the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date under subsection 150(1) for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. For corporations governed by paragraph 150(1)(a), because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, for a taxation year ending December 31, 2024, the absolute statutory deadline is June 30, 2026). Note that for Alberta's IEG (AT1 Schedule 29), the provincial deadline is 15 months after the AT1 filing due date (21 months after year-end), whereas British Columbia (Form T666) and federal SR&ED enforce the strict 18-month deadline. For individuals governed by subparagraph 150(1)(d)(ii), the tax return filing-due date is June 15 of the following year, resulting in an SR&ED reporting deadline of 17.5 months after the December 31 year-end (June 15 of the second following year). For trusts governed by paragraph 150(1)(c), the tax return filing-due date is 90 days after the trust's year-end, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of 15 months after the trust's year-end.

Crucially, subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act explicitly overrides the Minister of National Revenue's general fairness and taxpayer relief powers, prohibiting the CRA from granting any extension of time to file prescribed SR&ED forms or prescribed information past the 18-month statutory bar. If a claimant omits a project description, fails to list an expenditure on Form T661, or submits the claim one day after the 18-month deadline (unless the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, in which case it extends to the next business day), the claim is statutorily statute-barred and neither the CRA Appeals Branch nor the Tax Court of Canada has jurisdiction to grant equitable relief. While the CRA recommends filing the SR&ED claim concurrently with the T2 return within 6 months of year-end to accelerate cash refunds and preserve a 12-month window to file amended T661 forms, no new projects or increased expenditure lines can be added after the 18-month mark.

body.text: Form T661 Part 2 Technical Narratives and Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsection 162(5.1))

Two sections of Form T661 receive heightened scrutiny during initial screening and audit selection: Part 2, Section B (Project Descriptions) and Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information). In Part 2, Section B, for every claimed project, the claimant must answer three structured technical questions within strict statutory word-count limits—unless a federal agency has designated the project as "classified information" for national security reasons, in which case Section B is retained on a separate internal sheet and a formal notification letter is filed with the CRA SR&ED Directorate. First, Line 242 asks What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome? (subject to a maximum of 350 words), requiring the claimant to articulate the system-level technological limitation or knowledge gap that could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, Line 244 asks What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described on line 242? (subject to a maximum of 700 words), requiring a chronological summary of the systematic investigation or search detailing the explicit hypotheses formulated, experimental parameters tested, quantitative metrics analysed, and iterative modifications made during the specific fiscal year. Third, Line 246 asks What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described on line 244? (subject to a maximum of 350 words), requiring a concise statement of the new scientific or technological knowledge generated as a result of the investigation.

In Part 9 of Form T661, the claimant and any external "claim preparer" (any person or partnership that accepts consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim) must disclose the preparer's name, Business Number, billing arrangement code (such as contingency fee percentage, flat fee, or hourly rate), and total fee charged. Even if the claim was prepared entirely in-house without an external consultant, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9 certifying that no claim preparer was involved. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if prescribed claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate in Part 9, a strict $1,000 penalty is assessed—for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable.
CRA Service Standards, Pre-Claim Advisory Services, Audit Reviews, and Appeals

The CRA administers published processing service standards depending on whether a claim is accepted as filed or selected for review: refundable claims accepted without review are processed within 60 calendar days of receipt of a complete claim; claims that have undergone pre-claim approval are processed within 90 calendar days; refundable claims selected for technical and financial audit review have a service standard of 180 calendar days; and non-refundable claims are processed within 365 calendar days of receipt.

To mitigate audit risk prior to or immediately after filing, the CRA offers four free administrative support programs. First, the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) is an anonymous online diagnostic tool allowing businesses to test whether their R&D projects satisfy the "Why and How" eligibility criteria and estimate potential ITC refunds before preparing a claim. Second, the Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) and Pre-Claim Review (PCR) services—which replaced the legacy Pre-Claim Project Review (PCPR)—provide voluntary, on-demand evaluations by CRA SR&ED specialists while a project is still in progress or completed (provided it has not yet been reviewed and is not under objection or litigation), yielding written guidance on work eligibility and required contemporaneous documentation prior to filing Form T661. Third, the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) is triggered after a first-time claimant submits an initial SR&ED claim, providing an educational half-day consultation conducted by CRA technical and financial reviewers to advise the business on identifying eligible work, segregating allowable expenditures, and establishing compliant record-keeping systems for future taxation years. Fourth, the Account Executive (AE) Service assigns a designated CRA point of contact for recurring or complex corporate claimants.

When a filed claim is selected for a formal SR&ED audit review, the examination is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates scientific and technological eligibility under subsection 248(1)) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits payroll, T4 slips, specified employee caps, time tracking, contract agreements, and capital/lease logs under sections 37 and 127). If the RTA or FR proposes to disallow projects or expenditures in a draft SR&ED Review Report (Proposal Letter), the claimant navigates a structured four-stage dispute resolution pathway. In the first stage, within the 30-day response window to the Proposal Letter, the claimant submits a comprehensive written rebuttal to the RTA and FR supported by supplemental contemporaneous technical evidence—such as source-code commit histories, Jira tickets, experimental test logs, failed prototype data, and dated engineering notes—and legal submissions addressing the five questions of Northwest Hydraulic and Manning Canning Kitchens. If disagreement persists, the second stage allows the claimant to request an Administrative Second Review by escalating the file to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM) at the responsible Coordinating Tax Services Office (CTSO) to review procedural fairness and adherence to CRA policy before a Notice of Reassessment is issued. In the third stage, within 90 calendar days from the date printed on the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant exercises its statutory right under section 165 of the Income Tax Act to file a formal Notice of Objection (Form T400A) with the Chief of Appeals at the CRA Appeals Branch, triggering an independent review by an Appeals Officer assisted by an independent Technical Advisor not involved in the original audit. Finally, in the fourth stage, if the CRA Appeals Branch confirms the assessment or fails to render a decision within 90 days of the filing of the Notice of Objection, the claimant may file a Notice of Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under section 169 of the Act (electing the Informal Procedure for disputed federal tax and penalties up to $25,000 per year or the General Procedure for larger claims), with further appeal on questions of law to the Federal Court of Appeal.
Comprehensive Comparative Financial Modelling: Legacy vs. Post-Bill C-15 and CRIC Regimes

To illustrate the combined quantitative impact of the federal Bill C-15 legislative expansion and provincial tax credit interactions across different corporate profiles, the following table models three representative Canadian R&D scenarios for a taxation year beginning on or after April 1, 2025, where both federal Bill C-15 and Québec's CRIC are fully in force.

In Scenario A (Scaling Ontario AI & Hardware CCPC), the corporation incurs $4,000,000 in direct Ontario SR&ED salaries for arm's-length engineers and $500,000 in new dedicated GPU compute servers acquired after December 15, 2024 (used ≥ 90% ASA in SR&ED), while holding $30,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital from venture capital equity rounds alongside only $8,000,000 in three-year average gross revenue (and $0 prior-year taxable income); the corporation elects the Proxy Method (55% PPA) and elects the federal Gross Revenue Phase-Out Method. In Scenario B (Mid-Cap Québec Corporation Under CRIC), the corporation incurs $2,000,000 in direct Québec R&D salaries across 20 full-time R&D engineers (yielding an employee-based exclusion threshold of approximately $360,000) plus $400,000 in Québec pre-commercialization validation and homologation salaries across 4 engineers (exclusion threshold of approximately $72,000), while holding $100,000,000 in corporate assets and taxable capital (exceeding the $75 million federal capital and revenue phase-out thresholds) and electing the federal Proxy Method. In Scenario C (First-Year Alberta Cleantech CCPC with NRC IRAP Grant), the corporation incurs $1,000,000 in direct Alberta SR&ED salaries, receives a $400,000 non-repayable NRC IRAP wage grant, has a $0 two-year historical Alberta R&D spending base, and elects the Proxy Method.

body.text: Strategic Audit Defence and Tax Planning Recommendations

To maximize after-tax R&D yields and insulate claims against CRA and Revenu Québec audit adjustments under the 2025–2026 statutory regime, corporate tax directors and SR&ED practitioners should execute five core compliance strategies. First, every CCPC with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeding $15,000,000 across its associated corporate group must annually model its three-year average annual gross revenue under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.2) following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026. Because the revenue election is made on a year-by-year basis, capital-intensive corporations whose three-year average gross revenue is below $75,000,000 (or lower than their taxable capital) can preserve up to the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit and $2,100,000 in annual refundable federal ITCs, whereas high-revenue, asset-light software CCPCs whose gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000 while retaining less than $15,000,000 in taxable capital should remain on the default taxable capital method.

Second, because the Bill C-15 measures apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and to depreciable capital property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024), CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) that filed returns for fiscal periods beginning on or after December 16, 2024 prior to March 26, 2026 should immediately file amended Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 claims—strictly before their 18-month statutory reporting bar under subsections 37(11) and 220(2.2)—to capture restored capital expenditures, equipment lease costs, the doubled $6 million expenditure limit, and ECPC refundability. Third, to defend claims for depreciable capital property (Line 390; Boxes 780 and 782) and shared-use equipment (Line 504; Box 788) acquired after December 15, 2024, claimants must document at the point of acquisition (through board resolutions, capital expenditure requisitions, and engineering project plans) that the equipment is intended to be used for ≥ 90% (ASA) or > 50% (SUE) of its operating time in Canadian SR&ED, and maintain continuous machine-hour or GPU-utilization logs throughout the taxation year.

Fourth, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec claimants filing Form RD-1029.8.CR must rigorously segregate traditional R&D expenditures from pre-commercialization continuation expenditures (product design, homologation, and regulatory testing). While both streams qualify for the 30%/20% refundable Québec CRIC, only the R&D portion reported under Code 112 constitutes government assistance in respect of federal SR&ED on Lines 429 and 513 of federal Form T661, thereby shielding the federal ITC base against reduction by the Code 113 pre-commercialization credit. Fifth, when drafting Form T661 Part 2 narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246) and preparing for CRA RTA reviews, claimants must anchor every project description in the judicial standard of Northwest Hydraulic and Manning Canning Kitchens—framing technical narratives around system-level technological uncertainties that could not be resolved by routine engineering, explicitly demonstrating why publicly known tools, algorithms, or materials behaved unpredictably in the specific experimental context, and maintaining dated, iterative test records that link employee time sheets directly to each hypothesis tested.
